newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France's LVMH strikes back at GMG.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France's LVMH strikes back at GMG.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH, unhappy over the planned merger of Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, struck back on Wednesday by announcing plans to recover the full control of its champagne and cognac brands and push Guinness out of their lucrative distribution ventures.

LVMH said in a statement that it was entitled by a prior agreement with Guinness to buy its stakes in their joint distribution ventures as well as Guinness' 34 percent holding in LVMH's drinks operation Moet Hennessy as a result of the merger.

Analysts said a move by LVMH to take over the distribution ventures could undercut the benefits of the planned 24 billion pounds ($39 billion) Guinness-GrandMet merger by slashing the worldwide commercial sales network.
"Guinness wanted to develop synergies in this area with GrandMet, with GrandMet products distributed through its ventures and vice versa. That would now seem blocked," said one analyst.
But analysts said LVMH's threat appeared to be a tactical ploy to force Guinness and Grand Met to negotiate with LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault.
Guinness said LVMH had no legal right to exercise the options, and a spokesman for the British group said he was confident the merger would not be delayed.
But analysts said LVMH could delay the merger, which creates a food and drinks giant if the companies end up in a court battle.

"I think it will delay and disrupt the deal with lengthy legal proceedings in prospect, and the chances of it going ahead in its current form are now much reduced," said Charles Winston at HSBC James Capel.
Arnault opposed the Guinness-GrandMet merger on the grounds that only their drinks businesses were complementary.
LVMH, whose drinks portfolio includes Moet & Chandon, Veuve Cliquot and Pommery champagnes and Hennessy cognacs, owns 14 percent of Guinness.
It wanted Guinness to split its brewing and drinks activities and merge the drinks business, which includes Johnnie Walker whiskies, with Moet Hennessy to form a global leader.
"A similar proposal was made to Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, and this proposal remains open for discussion," LVMH said in its statement.
"What they (LVMH) want to do is merge the wines and spirits businesses and exit Pillsbury, Burger King and the beer business," said Cecile d'Estais at Paribas Capital Markets.
With 66 percent of Moet Hennessy and 14 percent of Guinness, LVMH would be the largest shareholder of that business.
But another analyst said he did not believe Arnault would get his way. "The boards of Guinness and Grand Met don't want any more of Arnault's demands. They've purposely marginalised him," he said.
In 1990, Guinness helped Arnault take over LVMH, but the two allies have since drifted apart, with LVMH focussing more on luxury goods and fretting about the return on its investment in Guinness.
It recently sold seven percent to help pay for the acquisition of the upscale Duty Free Shoppers chain.

LVMH said in its statement that the Guinness-GrandMet merger constituted a 'control event' relating to the ownership of Guinness, entitling LVMH to buy Guinness's interest in Moet Hennessy and in the joint ventures.

"As a result, LVMH will operate the joint ventures independently, with a right to continue to market and distribute on an exclusive basis Guinness brands...in the key markets of China, France, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States for at least 10 years," it said.
Guinness disputed LVMH's claim that the merger constituted a 'control event'.

"Guinness is confident that a 'control event' will not be triggered by the completion of the proposed merger, and that there is therefore no basis for the assertion made by LVMH," it said in a statement.
But the uncertainty weighed on Guinness' stock, which closed down 15-1/2 pence at 578-1/2. Grand Met shares fell 15 to 582.

Shares in LVMH initially rose on its announcement but closed down 1.63 percent, swept lower by a selloff on the bourse due to nervousness ahead of the parliamentary election on Sunday. The Paris bourse's blue-chip CAC index lost 3.63 percent. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
